html:
A collection of 124 letters by Seneca, written in the last years of his life, after he withdrew from Nero's court in 62 CE. They are addressed to his friend Lucilius, a Roman official in Sicily.

Each letter usually starts from something ordinary, such as a trip, a noisy bathhouse or an illness, and turns it into a lesson in Stoic living. The themes are practical: how to use time, why friendship matters, how to read, how to live with less, how to face death without fear. The first line tells Lucilius to "claim yourself for yourself" and stop letting time be stolen. Letter 47 asks that slaves be treated as fellow human beings. In the early letters Seneca often quotes Epicurus, from a rival school, because a good idea is good wherever it comes from.

The style is short, sharp sentences that are easy to remember. The letters were read through the Middle Ages and loved by Renaissance writers such as Montaigne. With the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, they are one of the main books of the modern revival of Stoicism.
